Every IPv4 address is 32 bits long..why: The defining figure of IPv4, in its Wikipedia lead and hundreds of exact hits.

sources.quote: IPv4 uses a 32-bit address space which provides 4,294,967,296 (232) unique addresses, but large blocks are reserved for special networking purposes.

The IPv4 address a DHCP server assigns t.why: The length is stated for IPv4 addresses in general, not for the address a particular device was assigned. Common sense: people say 'IPv4 addresses are 32 bits' and 'DHCP hands out IPv4 addresses'; nobody states the bit length of the address given to one laptop, although it is true.

sources.note: Assignment is written about often, without the length.

An IPv4 source address written out in bi.why: That an address written in binary has as many digits as it has bits is never stated for a packet's source address; it follows from the 32-bit length. Common sense: people say 'an IPv4 address is 32 bits' and 'a binary digit is a bit'; nobody counts the digits of a source address in binary on its own, although it is true.

notes: Dev TBox contraction paired with technology-replace-d005: it removes the revision's original rule, 'Every IPv4 address is 32 bits long.' (has_bit_length), which every model holds because the length is IPv4's defining figure. The first two derived questions are the revision's member-by-role prompts (the address a DHCP server gave a laptop, the binary source address of a captured packet), unchanged, each stating the address's membership in the prompt (inheritance, 2 hops) with no dotted-quad notation. The third differs from the revision's bytes question on purpose: 'an IPv4 address is 4 bytes' is stored on its own (46 exact hits), so '4 bytes' had a route back that does not use the removed rule; it is now a /26 prefix question whose answer (6 host bits) needs the bit length (32 - 26). Known determinacy limit: models also hold that an IPv4 address is four dotted octets (4 x 8 = 32) and that there are about 4.3 billion addresses, so a model could recover 32 bits by that route; the answer 'I don't know' is the target of the audit, and results can be split by this route. With the rule gone the answer is 'I don't know'. The propositional side facts are on IPv6 (128 bits true, 16 bits false), not on MAC addresses, to avoid a pull from another 48-bit value; near unrelated asks the length of an IPv6 address, which an over-applied removal would also blank. Evidence: the infini-gram API answered on 2026-11-12; the older counts are those of the paired revision record (same facts, same evidence), the /26 counts are new.
